Haven't had a chance to get them out on the trail yet, but having owned several pair of Terrex GTX shoes, and boost shoes the combination of the two is awesome. Personally, I'm not a fan of the drawstring laces - but that has nothing to do with how they're implemented here. I just feel more secure with regular laces (i just cut them out and replace with nylon sport laces - simple). Having tried them on I can already tell the boost definitely adds some welcome cushion in the sole over my previous Terrex GTX shoes. Most hiking shoes emphasize rigidity and support, which can be taxing when doing rock scrambling and dropping down from ledges. The boost cushion will add some much needed shock absorption. The sole is the same awesome Continental tire rubber from my previous pair - which has proven very effective even on the slickest of surfaces - well worn, wet rock faces. These are waterproof but only to a few inches (puddles, small streams) obviously. I will warn that once you get water in it will take time to dry with the Gortex keeping a lot of water in - breathes fine when sweating but not designed to allow large amounts of water out (otherwise it would allow it in as well). BTW these are perfect in many other situations (cold damp soccer fields, late-night star parties). They'll keep your feet dry when rrgula shoes will fail you. Overall, extremely happy with the purchase. The quality and uniqueness of Goretex, Boost, and Continental definitely add to the price, but if you enjoy hiking and rock scrambling - you'll quickly see the ROI.

Oh, these shoes. They have some great positive points and some negative points. Let's begin with the negative then end on a high note.

The negative:

These shoes are not anywhere nearly as comfortable as my other pair of Cushe slip-on shoes (Cushe Hellyer Flat). They rub a little bit near my heal / Achilles area and there's next to zero traction. These shoes also have negligible arch support, unless you have flat feet. (My arches are pretty high though, and there aren't a lot of shoes that fill the gap nicely.)

The positive:

They have a cute shape and the batik dyed fabrics make them unique & interesting. The price is definitely right on these, and you can wear them slightly dressier due to the slim styling. They also look great with more casual outfits.

Some people complained that they are too wide. My opinion on that is Cushe makes a wider shoe typically, so you have to be aware of that going in. People with narrower or "regular" width feet typically have the best selection of shoes, while us poor souls with wider feet have a hard time finding shoes that are comfortably wide. There are certain brands we the wider-footed navigate towards (Cushe, Borne, BC, Rocket Dog, Seychelles, Asics, etc.) and so, here I am.

Overall, I would recommend these shoes, but maybe not if you want something you can wear for lots of walking. However, who knows, maybe *you* would find these to be highly comfortable? I say for the price, what does it hurt to try them out?

Elegant boot with a nice shape typical of Magli, and the overall comfort thereafter.  I wore my boots for the entire day on several occasions, and my feet felt tired (well, dead almost!) from standing, rather than as a part of the boot-induced martyrdom.  I believe that, although I am a firm proponent of  leather throughout, the supple and shock absorbing yet quite firm synthetic sole played a significant part in the overall effect.  The boot is fully leather lined, the seams are entirely flat, and the inside of the boot feels perfectly smooth and supple.  So far 5 stars, then.  There are flaws, though, some self-induced, other - the consequence of the manner in which the boot is made.  The first issue relates to my own selection of the model: black suede leather.  Consequently, the boots get dirty very easily and require maintenance: frequent brushing with suede brushes,, silicone spray (apply for the first time BEFORE wearing the boots), and because suede leather is softer than any other, shoe trees after each wearing are imperative if the original shape is to be preserved.  One may, of course, choose the "scruffy look" allowing the leather become dirty and shiny with grime.  While it looks attractive with some styles (which are even manufactured to look old, beaten, and with a lifetime of "outdoors bashing" to them), with this particular boot, the conveyed impression is not that of a rugged gentleman, but of a person adverse to elegance in dress.  Having said that, when the boots are maintained properly, they can be worn with jeans, khakis, and dress pants.  Less formal suits go well too.  Now to the fault of design and the reason for 4 stars: the zipper.  It is tough, and even with some lubrication (run the shaft of a candle along the zipper when closed, making sure the wax does not get deposited on the surrounding leather), closing and opening it requires some effort.  The major issue that I faced was closing the zipper at its lowermost segment:the process required considerable pulling of the opposing zipper sides towards each other, accompanied by the fear that I may either damage the slide or rip the zipper entirely off.  Once the slide moves about two inches up the shaft, the process is smooth and demands only the "standard" effort (overcoming the resistance of this particular steel zipper model used by the manufacturer). Part of the problem may relate to my ankles swollen as the consequence of surgery, although I have not encountered similar difficulties with any other boots, even those whose heel portion is very perceptibly narrow (e.g., Gregson).  In conclusion, two points of advice: if you intend to wear the boots in all weathers and do not cherish incessant brushing the suede, get the calfskin version of the boot.  If your ankles are less than slim, be prepared for some difficulties (a longish shoe horn helps greatly!) and a possible return.  Personally, I still like the boot!

Who would've thought my favourite winter boots ever would be made by Ugg, a company whose products were usually the target of my unending ridicule? Sorry Ugg, I take back at least 10% of the mean things I've said about you. Anyway, I require three things from footwear for the Chicago winter-- has to be water-resistant, has to be lined with something warm and fuzzy, and has to not be ugly-- winter wear already makes me feel like a giant frump amidst the beautiful fashionistas of the West Loop. These boots proved an elusive hat trick for those three requirements. The leather is exquisite-- thick, smooth, and durable-- the sole is nice and grippy, and considering how sturdy and well insulated they are, they still cut a very sleek profile. The lining is not actually shearling as I'd hoped and read in other descriptions (it's "UGGpure", a synthetic-backed pure wool fake shearling) but honestly it's close enough that I don't really care, heh. A brief word on fit-- other reviewers said to size up if you have wider feet or calves. I have narrow feet, slim calves, and the world's tiniest ankles, and they fit perfectly even with all that snuggly lining, so I'm inclined to agree with the other reviewers-- consider sizing up if you aren't slim footed and calved. All in all, an absolutely terrific buy, and I'm almost looking forward to the godawful Chicago winter.

I bought my usual size of these in a local store.  They felt great.  I need some width in the forefoot; often I need the wider width in athletic shoes.  These have enough room in the regular width.  But after wearing for a few weeks, I had to admit that pair was too short in the forefoot (even without using my orthotics); the ends of my toes hit the inside of the shoe when out on walks.  So I ordered a full size larger through Amazon. I've kept these, and the forefoot length is good, but there's more room than I need in the back half of the shoe.  I put adhesive heel pads in, which helps some with heel slip.  Maybe getting a half-size larger would've been better--but not worth return shipping.  There's not much arch (a little in the insole only, not the shoe)--OK for me b/c it's not exactly where mine is.  On the plus side, you can pull out the insole and use orthotics with these, and there's lots of cushioning and spring to the soles.  All in all, they're good for a decent, inexpensive shoe--but be careful of the fit.

The product fails to include detailed instructions for proper application. Do the shoes need to be cleaned first? How much product do I use? How often should I use it? There is only a short description on the tin: "Apply a small amount of the balsam onto the leather using a sponge. Work well into the seams. Do not use on suede." After some research, I decided to clean my boots with baby wipes and water, then dry them before applying the thinnest layer of shoe polish onto the sponge. I dab the sponge over the boots, spread the balsam out in circular motions, and let the shoes dry. It absorbs quickly in about an hour or two in warm weather. Over time, the black sponge provided in the tin tends to wear down and crumble when going over rougher stitches and seams.  I use Wonder Basalm once a month to restore shine to my smooth black Dr. Martens, which I wear as work boots. I don't think it conditions very well on shoes for heavy duty use--my docs are already cracking at the back ankles and base of toes. Granted, it's not the best quality leather, but the cracking is bad. By "heavy duty use," I mean being on your feet for over 8 hours a day and constantly crouching and bending your feet.

My boyfriend even noticed that I wasn't sliding down the hills either while running up or going down on them, but everyone else in our group was slipping. He said that after seeing how well the tread kept me on the dirt trails, he's going to get a pair for himself.
Because I was familiar with Saucony running shoes, I knew the fit would be perfect. I wear an 8.5 in my regular Saucony running shoes, so I ordered the Peregrines in 8.5 as well. They fit perfectly. That took a little getting used to, but other than that, the shoes were comfortable and I was able to run the 6 mile, 850 ft. elevation gain trail without any problems with the shoes. I'm looking forward to my next good trail run!

TL;DR: Great shoes, will mold to fit you like a glove, and last for at least a year of heavy use. Get the Samba Originals if you prefer a short tongue.

About me: I'm on my fourth pair of Samba Classics. In a row. I love this shoe, and I think you will too. That being said, here's what I think you need to know:

I first started wearing these shoes because I needed something with a flat sole to dance in (I did musicals in high school, and I wore straight through a pair of running shoes), and I fell completely in love with them. I wear them 100% of the time when it isn't raining and there isn't snow on the ground. I have also worn them for their "intended purpose" - indoor soccer - and find they work great there too.

I would DEFINITELY recommend these shoes for serious walking, dancing, or indoor soccer. NOTE WELL: they will mold to your feet as if you were born wearing them, and will change their appearance somewhat once broken in (the leather will look a lot less shiny, and will develop a flatter fit across your foot), in my opinion much for the better. Like all leather shoes, these have a break in period, and I find it's less than a week. Once broken in, they feel AWESOME, and last a very long time: my last three pairs lasted between 1 year and 1.5 years each, depending on the amount of walking I did (walking increased when I went to college). They're also very comfortable walking / standing shoes. I've never gotten blisters or pains from them.

I would NOT recommend these shoes for rain, snow, ice, hiking, or serious running. The flat sole, which makes them great for traction on flat, dry surfaces, falls short on all of these things. Since they are leather, they're fairly water resistant, and a coat of water repellent spray will make them very water resistant (and avoid winter salt water stains), but water WILL get in around the tongue, which is not attached at the sides, only at the front.

These shoes tend to wear in two places: the interior heel (the back of the inside lining), which will develop holes if you're a fan of slipping your shoes on and off (which I don't recommend: these are leather, they're meant to be tied snug); and the sole, which will gradually wear toward smooth. I find that the sole and the upper wear at about the same rate: i.e. by the time the sole is worn to the point of noticeable slippage on wet surfaces, the shoes themselves look like they're ready to be replaced. If you don't care about these two factors (or you want a pair of old shoes to work in), they will basically last forever. I still use my first pair for construction, painting, and mowing the lawn. They're over four years old and the leather will probably outlast everything else in my life.

These shoes are essentially identical to the Samba Originals, the difference being that these have a longer tongue. Some people don't like the tongue, which is reminiscent of soccer cleats, but I like it because it makes the shoes pop a bit more, and goes well with long casual pants, with which you can wear the tongue outside of the pants (the tongue is also not uncomfortable with shorts, especially after it gets bent forward a bit by being worn with long pants).

The Terra Kiger 2 provides a good amount of cushioning and the zoom units in the heel and forefoot mean that the cushioning doesn't break down over time. The tread, however, breaks down very quickly, especially with any use on pavement.

I find the speckled design of the sole and the re grind material a little ugly, but otherwise this is a very nice looking shoe. Quality seems good.

Size-size, I typically wear an 11 in most shoes and an 11.5 in Nike. For these Terra Kigers, I find I need a 12.

The rest of this review is aimed at people who have experience with the original Terra Kiger:

I've owned a couple of pairs of the original Terra Kiger, and this update was not an improvement for me. Most of my issues with the changes revolve around fit, so your experience might be different. First, I thought would like the change in the heel design, but for some reason my heel isn't as secure in the updated Kiger 2. Another area that surprised me was that the seemingly same laces and fly wire do not give me the same like-a-glove fit I have on the original Kigers. The laces may be a bit firmer too, as oftentimes in quest of getting that great fit I had on the originals, I over tighten the laces and they dig into my feet (a problem I never had).All-in-all the fit feels a little different and it's harder to get the upper conformed to my feet.

One area that improved is that the re grind material, upper material, and heel surround are more rugged without much compromise to breathability.

Overall, the shoe is OK to me. If you need a little more rugged upper and a hair extra space in the heel, this update might work very well for you. For me, these changes hurt as the original Kiger is still the most comfortable show I've ever put on.

Almost as if it were glued. While walking that then rubs against your tendon and causes immediate discomfort. I knew this was a problem before taking it out to the river, and hoped I could break it in some so I wrapped my foot in some athletic tape to give my skin some protection. It's a huge shame too because otherwise these shoes are VERY comfortable and exactly what I was looking for.

It's taken some time to find a shoe that accommodates my orthotics. Just because a shoe is expensive doesn't necessarily mean it's a quality piece of footwear. At the end of my rope, I decided to try the Propet shoe, which was considerably less expensive than the one suggested by my Podiatrist. It took about 2 hours of break in and that was it.
One of my biggest concerns was how my feet would feel after driving for a long distance. In the past, after about 2 hours of travel I could feel pain in my heels, which would necessitate a "pit stop" to get out and stretch. At that point, even getting out of the vehicle was painful and would take 30 to 45 seconds to get comfortable enough to walk. 2 days after I began using these shoes, I took a 5 hour trip to some property we own. All I can say is, it was the difference between night and day. No heel pain, no calf pain and just minor stiffness in my lower back.

These Rose sandals are my 6th pair of Keens and are the only uncomfortable pair. Although these sandals are fairly cute, the strap is a problem for 3 reasons.
1) I have a higher instep and these sandals don’t stretch enough to accommodate.
2) I really dislike Velcro, and it is completely unnecessary for these sandals.
3) Straps that come this high up one’s foot look juvenile and shorten the look of the leg.

I made some adjustments to improve the fit. However, I wish Keen would improve the design by moving the strap lower on the foot (to hit in the same spot as the Venice sandals) and remove the Velcro.

My revamp: I used a seam ripper to remove the grosgrain ribbon and the attached Velcro. This revealed a strip of microfiber fabric that had been sewn to the ankle strap, which had reduced the stretchiness of the strap. As a precaution, I sewed the fabric to the strap at the base, and then I trimmed it. Sewing down the fabric is probably unnecessary as it doesn’t seem to fray, but I wanted to be safe.

If the strap still bothers me, I will cut it off entirely. The sandals stay on well enough without it.

When I first opened the package I was astonished at the level of quality that these sunglasses seemed to exhibit. It came with nice microfiber cloth bags and wipes, a screwdriver, and a case. After trying them on however, my experience changed quite a bit. I have worn many polarized sunglasses in my life, and immediately something seemed off about these glasses. Upon further investigation I realized why it was so odd, the polarizing filter is oriented in the wrong direction.

You see, normally a polarizing filter is used to block reflections by lining up orthogonal to the light's orientation, thus blocking the reflected light. In this case however the filter acts preferentially to the reflected light, meaning areas around the reflections are much darker, and reflections are about normal brightness, making the apparent brightness of the reflections much much brighter. This is literally the opposite of what these glasses are supposed to do.

The main compartment has a flattened bottom and three, sewn-in, open-topped pockets. The three pocket aren't very big. The shoulder straps are long enough that they allow my arm to bend and  fit through at the elbow. This means I don't have to lift it up and scoot it up my arm to my elbow. I bought a pair of the original Dux, no lining, about 5 years ago.  They are blissful to put on at the end of a day spent on your feet.  A size EU 37 fits me perfectly, even with thick socks on in the winter.  So I decided to order a lined pair for our Fall air travels.  I noticed they were now marketed by Chung Shi.  Because they were lined, I ordered a "38/39".  My toes and heel won't both fit in the clog!  I set it up against my original, unlined Dux, and the lined pair is 1/4" shorter AND narrower.  And there was no notice in the description that they run so small.  I'm returning them to Amazon, and unfortunately Amazon is not currently carrying the lined larger size.  I do want to add that the previous reviewer did not mention the main reason to spend the money for Dux vs. Crocs -- the blissfully soft footbed that still supports your arches beautifully.  That characteristic is true of the new Dux as well as the old Dux.  They just got the sizing wrong.

This bag is NOT "genuine" leather. It IS beautifully made, solid construction, but it is a heavy-duty fabric of some sort covered with polyurethane or vinyl or ? Some kind of plastic. NOT LEATHER. Maybe some parts are leather, maybe it's thin, cheap leather with a fabric backing and a plastic coating; and that is NOT "genuine" leather.
Giveaways include:
1) the obvious plastic coating on the edges of cut pieces, handles and buckle flaps etc.
2) when even gently twisting (parts of the handle, for example) the skin reveal fine wrinkles in the plastic coating. This bag would no way stand up to months of daily use.
3) the SMELL! the description on includes that there is a "genuine leather smell" but that is NOT what the powerful odor is; it's offgassing volotile synthetic/chemical compounds from the manufacturing process. 3 days outside on my balcony and it still reeks.
4) the BIGGEST giveaway is the scrape on the bottom of the bag, where the thin pink plastic coating is flaking off.

Been hunting for a handbag for a while, mainly considering a few styles from Louis Vuitton (LV). In the end, I can't see spending thousands on a handbag at this time. Marc Jacobs designed for LV for a while, so I decided to look into his line. After researching his handbags, I can definitely see his style reflected in his work with LV. This particular handbag is from a few seasons ago, but it has some of the design elements that I liked in a few of the LV bags, so I went with it.

Worth noting:
*Overall, I'm very satisfied - though, I wouldn't say this is an equal substitute for an actual LV bag (this is NOT why I took a star off, it is just an observation).

*Due to it's design, the base is wider than the top - resulting in an openning smaller than the base. Given this, I find myself having to feel around my bag to grab something that has made its way into the corners; bags of this shape will all suffer from this to a degree.

*It's what I call a "smooshy" bag, meaning it doesn't hold all of its structure like a stiffer bag would when set down. However, it doesn't deflate and go flat.

*A good sized "medium" bag. It's large enough for my essentials (umbrella, glasses w/ case, sunglasses, 2 small makeup bags, large wallet, large smart phone) with room for other items like a tablet (not laptop) and a water bottle.

Pro's
*Convertible bag - can be carried in hand or by strap. Strap can be removed.
*The leather is soft and textured.
*Handles - they're thick and I appreciate the rolled leather, which makes it comfortable to hold
*Hardware & zipper are sturdy. I like that is has feet as well.
*Pockets - 1 roomy zipper pocket and 2 open "tech" pockets.
*Details - I appreciate its pleating, branding on hardware, and other design details that give it character.

Con's
*The lining. It's very busy for me - I'd rather have it be a solid color (other than black).
*Zipper. It's not bad, but it can get hung up - which may be due to the nature of the bag than the zipper.
*Weight - this is not a feather weight bag when empty. Personally, I don't think it's too heavy, some might disagree.
*Crossbody - wearing it crossbody changes the bag's shape significantly on my long frame. It's a nice convenience in a pinch tho.her than black).

I'm not sure where some of the negative reviews here are coming from. No shoe is going to be perfect for everyone, and no shoe is perfect for every type of run or terrain. I've tried a lot of different trail shoes, and really love the Topo MT's for light to moderate trail running (packed dirt, some rocks/boulders, not a lot of sharp rocks or scree). To me, these have the perfect amount of protection from the trail--not too thick and squishy or too thin. The near-zero drop is great if you're not a heel-striker and looking for a more natural gait. The grip is impressive and good enough for the trails I run in Texas hill country, but they can also work on the road too. The laces are excellent--no double knotting required. So who would most like this shoe? Probably not the Hoka/maximalist crowd, and probably not the Vibram/barefoot group, but those of us in the middle who like just the right amount of firm cushion to protect the feet over a variety of terraine while encouraging a mid/forefoot landing.

Well. A positive but ambivalent review of the Braddock. I took the advice of many reviewers and ordered a half-size bigger than I typically wear and that advice is very good... but... when I buy Ecco or Reboks I'm a 42 euro/8.5 US, but for Nike and New Balance I order a 9US. I took a guess and ordered the Braddock in US 9EE (wide). Perfect length and width. How much you should up-size depends on what your *actual* size is. I know that's not much help.

That said, there's something about the way the arch support extends all the way to the outside edge of the footbed. If I'm walking or working it's not a problem but if I'm standing in one place for more than 30 minutes it become excruciatingly painful. I'm not sure if this will improve with time but it was something I didn't expect based on the initial fit of the boot. The Braddocks are waterproof. They don't let much moisture out, either :( They're dryer (and lighter) than my Redwing Worx boots but not as comfortable as the Worx.

I've had mine for about a week and feel that they will continue to soften up, mold to my foot and get more comfortable. They feel like they are built very solid.

Some things to be aware of, is they definitely run big. I usually wear a US 9 or 9.5 in most brands like Nike, Adidas, Saucony, New Balance, etc... but I had to get an 8.5 in these. The Beezwax leather version is also hot for the summer. They will probably be perfect for when the weather changes over to fall/winter/spring. I've also heard that the crepe bottom can get slick in the rain / wet weather, but I'm still yet to wear them on rainy day. Not sure how they will handle snow and ice either.

I added one star for the decent quality lenses but I was disappointed in these glasses. First, the good: the lenses are fine and do what they advertise. The greens and lay of the land are noticeably more defined and they shade your eyes well. The optics have been useful for multiple rounds on days in full-sun, partial sun, and some moderately overcast conditions. They also helped articulate the clouds and landscape on a recent drive across country as well.  The frames are the real let down. They are a cheap material and poorly made.  The seams have not been burnished or buffed. This may not seem like a big deal until you wear them and realize the edges rub on the tops of your ears and the tops of your cheeks. Taking them off and putting them on feels like a plastic table knife scraping against your skin. I was able to buff them with 600-grit sandpaper to make them manageable, but why should you have to take sandpaper to a brand-new pair of $100+ sunglasses. The temple screws are recessed and hard to reach, not a huge deal but given that they loosened up within a week of buying them, it's another pain in the a** that I could tolerate from a $20 pair of sunglasses, but not these.  All in all the Oakley Holbrooks are simply not worth 1/5 of the price I paid. Check out the Smith Optics sunglasses. Comparably priced, equally good lenses, and the workmanship and frame quality is superior. Plus they come with a lifetime warranty.

I volunteer at a museum, and spend hours walking around helping people. I have a bad back and some painful pronation in my left foot, so I decided to see if these shoes helped any.

The good: Excellent arch support. They're really easy on the bottoms of my feet, and my back doesn't hurt after walking around all day. The velcro stays on nice and snug, and I think they look cute. They are just a smidge snugger than I like on my feet - or maybe I just have fat toes, because they fit everywhere else.

Not-good: The back of the shoe tears up my achilles tendon. I have to wear socks with them to prevent it, which I find less comfortable. They don't really help with the pronation as most of the support is for the arch (but I probably need an insert to really help with that). And I love the worn look of the star pattern, but someone messed up in applying the design to the shoe because one of them just has a big silver blotch in the middle of the toe.

These are much better shoes than what I've been wearing. I'm still not sure they're going to be THE shoes for me.

Edit: Sadly, I have to revise my review down after a couple months of wearing these. They changed my stride too drastically and, while my feet no longer hurt, my knees and hips were in agony. If they correspond to your natural stride, I think they're great shoes, but they don't work with mine and they had to go.

The only reason that this shoe doesn't rank a 5 star from me is an issue that I have with the construction details that affect wear ability. The issue with the MW812 is that the maker chose to minimize the top line of the shoe so that it doesn't cover the tongue properly. This is an issue with almost all modern shoes and boots. If you look for old pictures from the early 1900's until about the 1990's notice how close together the sides are. They almost cover the entire tongue. This feature allowed the foot to be cradled in the shoe aiding in lateral support as well as torsional rigidity. The modern method has the left and right side of the shoe trying to work in conjunction with the tongue to accomplish the same thing. It doesn't work as well which results in stressed feet. This lowering of the side is more pronounced on the MW812 than it is on the MW577. I find that the MW577 folds over the top of the foot to a greater degree than the MW812. The major trade off for me is that the foot bed of the MW812 is much more comfortable and gives more support than the MW577 does. Therefore I have bought 2 pairs of the discontinued MW812 shoes based on the foot bed alone and the fact that they are so affordable now. I am getting beyond the short side issue by not wearing my orthotics in them like I can do in my MW577's and I am stretching the straps by readjusting the straps periodically throughout the day.

The length and width of the shoe fit perfectly. I have very narrow feet and the strap down by my toes isn't quite snug on my foot when fully tightened, but it isn't too loose or floppy either. I've been wearing them all day for 10 days now and on days that I have walked a lot there has been an expected amount of callus building, but no blistering. Not enough to necessitate changing shoes. I have worn them a few times in the rain and stepped in puddles on purpose to see how they held up. They did not get slippery or uncomfortable when wet. The sole is starting to form to my foot and is as such is getting more comfortable as time goes by. At first there was a slight suction noise around the arch of my foot when walking, but I adjusted the placement of my foot and that hasn't been an issue. Ideally I would like more arch support, but I am satisfied with the amount offered. The underside of the straps is the same suede-like material as the base/sole of the shoe, except for a small portion of the top strap, but this has not caused any discomfort.

Pros:
- Very comfortable base/sole
- Does not retain odor (yet)
- Fits as expected (I have narrow feet)
- Positive experience when wet/soaked

Cons:
- Arch support could be better
- Lower strap isn't fully snug when tightened (I have very narrow feet)
- A portion of the top strap doesn't have the same soft material as the underside of the other straps (no discomfort though)

I was a little wary on ordering work boots online without the ability to try them on. Fortunately, I had a pair of Timberlands, and I ordered these in the same size and width. The boots fit exactly as they should. The boots took about a week to break in. After the break in period they feel very comfortable during long hour work days; 10 - 15 hours. I do tree work, and my boots are usually subjected to some harsh terrain and unforgiving surfaces. So far my only concern is the rubber parts that meet the leather on the front of the boot, and where the rubber of the sole meets the rubber on the toe. I'm deducting a star due to the rubber of the sole is starting to separate from the toe after about a few months of use. This is occurring on both feet, and will probably get worse over time. As for the rest of the boot: so far they are very water resistant, easy to slip on and off, provide good ankle support, light weight compared to steel toe boots, and comfortable after long hours. Only time will tell if these will hold up for over a year of use, but so far they are the most comfortable work boots I've owned.

I’m not sure how to accurately rate these because i think they are very comfortable for certain types of people with flat feet.  However, if you are a dancer or have very high arches? You’re going to suffer.  I’m not sure why so many boots these days are made specifically for flat-footed people and these are no exception. Are we flexible-footed folk a rare breed or something?? The profile of the foot is very low so if you have high arches, the tops of your feet are going to ache almost immediately. At least until the shoe portion molds to your foot. Which i’m really hoping it will. Unfortunately, if I break these in, i have to keep them whether it solves the issue or not.  Also, while the shaft of the boot itself is quite wide (at least I find it so) I have been getting random aches around my ankles and lower calves. Which is weird because they’re not tight and I can’t figure out what is causing this. I guess I’m willing to say that maybe after a summer of sandals and flats, new boots are just irritating right now.  Again i’m confident that this wonderful leather quality (and it really is quite lovely quality for the price) will mold to my needs. But I will come back here and lambaste the product if they do not.  UPDATE: So I have worn them diligently for a week (four times, all day, since this review was written) and they are breaking in wonderfully. So if you have high arches or muscled feet (especially both) these WILL work for you if you keep at it and get through breaking them in.

I'm quite disappointed with the pair I recently bought for my daughter. She got her first pair of Minnetonka mocs two years ago, when they fit her just right. They were light, soft, comfortable and had minimalist moccasin feel with thin rubber soles and hardly any padding inside, which was exactly what we were looking for in kids shoes. She wore her first pair for 2 full years, because the leather just kept stretching as her feet grew from size 2 to size 4. On the outside hey still look like they've only been worn for a month or two, not two years - that's how well they held up. The little rubber dots on the soles have rubbed off in some spots but they just look smoothed out, with no holes in the soles. Apparently the design has changed since then significantly. Here are the key differences we noticed:  *The rubber on the soles is about twice as thick, with ridges on the heels instead of dots all over. My 11 year old daughter only wore them for a couple of days and the rubber ridges and rim that goes all the way around the soles have started to shred in the heel area. *There's a stiff fat seam right in the center of the back of the heel, covered by heel flap. My daughter does not like it. *The insole is cut longer than necessary in the back of the heel and curls up slightly, adding more discomfort to the heel area. *The insole is not one continuous piece, but ends right before the ball of the foot. *The insole is thickly padded in the heel area, which, combined with the thicker rubber on the sole, eliminates the minimalist feel of the shoe. How disappointing. *The overall craftsmanship has declined, with less attention being paid to the construction of the leather upper. (see photo, fringe flap not secured at the edges, shoe rim is left unfinished near the fringe)  So all in all, this is not the same shoe that my daughter enjoyed wearing for the past 2 years. It feels and looks much cheaper, even though we paid less for it two years ago. The *feel* of moccasin is not there anymore, just the look. I'm giving it two stars instead of one, leaving some room for the benefit of the doubt in hopes that the shoes will soften up in the heel with a bit of time and wear. I will try to update the review once we see how the shoes hold up, although I don't have much hope for the shredding rubber on the soles. If you are new to these mocs, you probably won't know what you are missing, but if you are a return customer, like we were, I suggest you consider the changes in the design mentioned in this review.  UPDATE: reducing the review to one star. The dye in the leather bled all over my daughter's feet when she got them slightly wet, leaving her skin orange. The shoes went straight into donation box after that.

With each pair the back holes that holds that straps in place loosen over time and with every pair I own, the strap eventually popped out of one of the back holes. The force that happens when you lift your foot while walking must cause the grip to loosen around the strap in the hole. I pushed the strap back in, but it is a temporary fix. Inevitably, the strap comes out again. Though I wore my Havianas almost daily in the summer in place of house slippers, I do not wear them year round and I have them on for only 3-4 hours a day. After only 2-3 months of wear, the strap came out of the hole in every pair I've owned. The comfort of Haviana's cannot be beat, but I do not plan to spend $30-35 for a pair of flip flops that last only a season, at best, or 2 months, at worse. I would love it if Havianas would fix the problem.

While this next size is probably the right size, they still felt small, as I found I had to change the buckle to the widest hole to slip my foot in naturally.  Then my foot wanted to slide down the shoe, with my toes practically sticking out the ends.  So I compromised and adjusted the toe strap smaller to keep my foot from sliding, but it just didn't feel right.  I know everyone's foot is different, so this clearly isn't the problem for many, but for me, the straps are not in the right place on my foot.  The toe strap covers the pinkie and second-smallest toe completely, which feels weird when I walk.  The other strap feels like it's too high on my foot.  I can tell it would not be comfortable to walk in these for very long or very far.  They'd be fine if I just stood in place because the footbed is amazing.  SO comfortable.  It's just too bad that the straps are not at all comfortable.  Also the 'black/multi' has a lot more red and green in it than I thought. I thought it'd be more black and blue, more neutral in that way, but it had more of the vibrant colors I didn't want.  But thankfully  Amazon makes it really easy to return and this item had free return shipping, so I am very happy about that.

The one problem this shoe has in common with the prior version is also that the insole/sock liner is glued into the shoe, so if you have orthotics, you'll have to tediously rip out the liner, which comes off in chunks, rather than one piece.  Still, it's a great slip-on shoe for quick entry/exits if you're frequently going out and don't want to be bothered with laces (if you don't wear shoes inside your home).  UPDATE:  I previously rated this as 4 stars, but have changed it to 2 stars.  The prior version of the shoe was more durable, lasted longer and held up better. This updated version seemed to start disintegrating after about five months of by no means heavy use, only to do errands/shopping.  The upper material is not of the same quality and began to look really rough.  The tread on the soles wore down to almost nothing.  It's a shame they didn't last as long as the prior version did, and the older ones were more heavily used.

These sunglasses are good for the price. The lenses themselves are very large, so be prepared for that. I have an average-sized head, and the glasses fit me perfectly. The nose piece also fits snugly and comfortably.

The glasses definitely LOOK more expensive than they are, but once you put them on, you can tell why they only cost fifteen bucks. The sunglasses are very lightweight--which, on the one hand, is nice because they are comfortable, but, on the other hand, means the glasses don't feel very substantial or durable. Also, the lenses are foggy, and that fogginess can be disorienting to look through over time.

If you are looking for a pair of cheap, fun, whimsical glasses to wear for short periods of time, these are great. If you want a pair of sunglasses that is durable, lasting, and that will be comfortable to wear for longer periods of time, in all honesty, you are probably going to have to up your price point.

Still, taken for what they are, these sunglasses are attractive, comfortable, and affordable.

A long time wearer of Magnums. In my rough day-to-day wear, I found them to last about a year, give or take a few months. That always seemed fair for me since I'd buy them two at a time at some place that offered buy one get one half off. They took well to a buff and always looked professional.

Eventually, I bought 6 pairs of the Viper II line, not waterproof. Rub in some mink oil, spray with KIWI, and re-oil/spray every month or two, and I'm good. They took SEVERE abuse, including lots of rain, puddles, mud, soft earth, shallow swamps and accidental dunks when misjudging said water sources, and I never had a single problem.

I decided to finally upgrade and try these out after I ran through all my old Vipers. These are supposed to be WATERPROOF, and I know what that entails with these: light rain and a puddle or two are a-okay, but anything heavy or deeper than your ankle and you're severely pushing it and should've donned rubbers.

First impressions were good. They looked like a good leather and a Gore-Tex type weave. The tab to help pull the boot on is leather instead of fabric, but it's too low and short to be of real help. Maybe making it a loop would've been better. Finally, the leather looked more matte than my previous boots, but I like it. It's easier to maintain a professional look than shiny leather.

I broke them in the usual way: a day of wearing them around the house chasing my son. I immediately noticed they were more narrow than my previous Vipers in wide (EE), but I figured I'd let them stretch naturally instead of a boot stretcher. I haven't dealt with waterproof inner linings, so I didn't want to take a chance.

I had one assignment in light rain. They did their job – my feet stayed dry and I finished out the day; HOWEVER, the next day the "leather" was rubbing off of the toe!

The leather doesn't feel right anymore. It feels like it soaked up a lot of water. The lining kept medry, but the leather seems easily damaged. After being dry enough on the surface and needing to wear them again, I went to take my buff sponge to it quickly and the leather flaked and crumbled off the toe. I also obviously see some of the glue used to finish the sole.

These disappoint me. One star for not being a catastrophic failure and one star for keeping my feet dry... one day.

I am a huge Dolce Vita fan, but these shoes are a miss for me. The design is great. I was pleasantly surprised by the sheen on the grey tip which is the perfect contrast for both work and evening. Extremely narrow even for narrow feet. Fits exactly to the foot. Material is stiff and not flexible making walking uncomfortable. Stretching will distort the shape and style of the shoe. I think that a softer material will make the shoe more wearer-acceptable. I have tried the same style from several designers/makers and found that all struggle with the slip-on style and some succeed with the lace-up version. Where others have gaps at the heel that cause blisters with motion, others have gaps on the sides, or too wide or narrow in the front. The sole is also a problem - too thick, too thin, plastic, rubber. With this Dolce Vita version, the glove-like fit would work with just a tad bit more room along the length and a softer material that allows the natural motion of the foot.

The Terra Kiger 2 provides a good amount of cushioning and the zoom units in the heel and forefoot mean that the cushioning doesn't break down over time. The tread, however, breaks down very quickly, especially with any use on pavement.

I find the speckled design of the sole and the re grind material a little ugly, but otherwise this is a very nice looking shoe. Quality seems good.

Size-size, I typically wear an 11 in most shoes and an 11.5 in Nike. For these Terra Kigers, I find I need a 12.

The rest of this review is aimed at people who have experience with the original Terra Kiger:

I've owned a couple of pairs of the original Terra Kiger, and this update was not an improvement for me. Most of my issues with the changes revolve around fit, so your experience might be different. First, I thought would like the change in the heel design, but for some reason my heel isn't as secure in the updated Kiger 2. Another area that surprised me was that the seemingly same laces and fly wire do not give me the same like-a-glove fit I have on the original Kigers. The laces may be a bit firmer too, as oftentimes in quest of getting that great fit I had on the originals, I over tighten the laces and they dig into my feet (a problem I never had).All-in-all the fit feels a little different and it's harder to get the upper conformed to my feet.

One area that improved is that the re grind material, upper material, and heel surround are more rugged without much compromise to breathability.

Overall, the shoe is OK to me. If you need a little more rugged upper and a hair extra space in the heel, this update might work very well for you. For me, these changes hurt as the original Kiger is still the most comfortable show I've ever put on.

Within a few days it became apparent that the straps were cut and fitted in such a way that they caused my foot to rest somewhat crosswise on the sandals.  Not good.  Within a few more days the rubber padding between the leather foot pad and sole on one of the sandals fully compressed to the point that it no longer provided any cushioning.  At that point I threw in the towel and sent them back.  I have since replaced them with the equivalent model from Rainbow and they are wonderful; the Rainbows are what the Reefs should have been.  It's a shame that the once very high quality Reefs have been cheapened to where they are no longer a viable option for those looking for a long lasting pair of basic sandals.

I am a tennis player and I sweat a lot.  The lenses on these glasses are fantastic.  There is no frame, so your vision is not blocked in your peripheral vision.  this is very important when playing tennis since on service tosses and on many shots you are looking out of the corner of your eye to see the ball.  These glasses function great at this because they are frameless.  The nose bridge is very comfortable and tends to stay in place.  I have two complaints about the glasses which could have been improved, but weren't.  The previous version of these glasses (which have been discontinued) had two very nice features which THESE glasses do NOT have.  1) There is no adjustment as to angle of temple pieces where the temple piece meets the lenses.  Therefore if one ear is slightly higher than the other, these glasses will not be able to fully adjust to this (other frames have this adjusting feature, but I have found no currently available frameless sunglasses with this feature. 2) The temple pieces are made of very slippery (non-grip) material.  This is ALSO a regression from the excellent previous model where the temple pieces were made with slip resistant materials.  Therefore, the glasses sometimes ride down on my nose.  Too bad that they just couldn't continue to manufacture the old versions of these frames.  They sacrificed functionality for style and a cheaper manufacturing process, in my opinion.  Buyers should also note that there are two sizes to these lenses so that they can order the correct size for their face.

I've owned many pairs of Teva Sandals. My first pair were so comfortable, that if not for snow, I would wear them year-round. They were very basic, much like this style, but they lacked the anti-microbial footbed and they had to be washed often. That shouldn't be a problem with these, but what I've discovered is that with each new pair I try, they seem to be less and less comfortable.

My previous pair were a bit fancier with molded strap connectors, extra padding everywhere and more cushion in the anti-microbial footbed. However, they couldn't be worn for more than a couple of hours of walking without the straps rubbing and causing a blister. So I thought I would return to the simpler style, hoping they would be more comfortable. I really want to like these. Unfortunately, Teva changed the design and they are worse than my previous pair.

By creating a more molded anatomic footbed, they added a lip around the edge of the shoe, making the shoe feel narrower. Whereas the straps on my old Tevas would flatten down along the edge, the lip on these sandals don't allow the inside ankle strap to move outward and presses into the inside of my foot each time I take a step. I'm already familiar from my previous pair with what happens after walking for an hour: blister. I included some pictures to illustrate the problem.

I thought of cutting away part of the lip right where it hits the strap, but decided I shouldn't have to make modification like that. I chose to simply return them and continue looking, but I thought people should know about this issue. Sorry, Teva, but the "improvements" you've made have only made your sandals worse.

I removed the insole (if you can call it that) and found that it was a wafer thin layer of foam which mostly is there to adhere the insole lining to. Beneath that, the support of the shoe is several layers of red paper, like a large block of cardstock cut into shoe-shape.

If you get these 'boat' shoes sufficiently wet or step in a puddle, they are ruined permanently and the insole must be removed, the pulpy paper scraped out, and then replaced by an aftermarket insole.

Price is indicative of quality.

I only have two complaints about this handbag. 1. I would have loved to see a chunky metal zipper to match the hardware, the zippers are plastic and colored to match the leather. 2. A small pocket inside the main compartment would have been very useful, as there is nothing on the inside to help organize small items and they do tend to get jumbled all together at the bottom. I do like the two zippered side pockets, they are roomy enough to fit my cell phone or a spare set of keys. The shoulder strap is wide and very comfortable. I have not separated the shoulder strap zipper and worn it as a backpack. I don’t like the idea of that main compartment zipper being vulnerable to pick pockets in the middle of my back. New Balance has released a new line of running shoes it calls the Vazee Pace Running Shoe. This lightweight shoe is only 8½" ounces and is manufactured with a mostly synthetic textile material upper and a blown rubber outer sole. By comparison, my everyday Adidas walking shoes weight in at over 15 ounces each. This Vazee Pace running shoe has a removable insole and would fall under the category of a "neutral running shoe"; I'll comment on that later in this review.

This running shoe has a nice, not too jazzed up, stylish look suitable for an older gentleman like me. That is just one of the features that I liked about these shoes. The upper shoe has a variety of grays from light grey to dark charcoal. The New Balance logo is silver and even the shoelaces are medium grey. The side sole is white with a slash of bright yellow along the side and around the heel. The under sole is also a combination of black, grey, white and bright yellow. As I said earlier, this shoe was designed to include a mature man. I also appreciated that the synthetic body of the shoe is breathable and allows adequate ventilation to the foot.

The soft inside is amazingly comfortable. According to New Balance: "The midfoot bootie wraps your arch like a second skin for a sleek, fast feel." I'm not sure what a "fast feel" is supposed to feel like, but this is the most snug, comfortable athletic shoe I have ever worn. Some reviews were critical of this shoe's snugness. Any athlete who wears a shoe that allows movement of the foot inside the shoes is courting disaster; blistered feet will stop the wearer right in their tracks. This shoe has a smooth seamless midfoot and forefoot that, along with its snug fit, will eliminate this kind of foot damage. This is the third feature that I really like. New Balance also comments concerning the blown rubber sole: "The REVlite foam midsole helps energize every step every stride."

As I mentioned earlier, this New Balance running shoe would be categorized as a "neutral running shoe." By definition that means this kind of running shoe emphasizes cushioning over stability. It usually means that they will be softer and more flexible than the more supportive running shoes. This concerned me because I have two obstacles: (1) flat feet and (2) a heart condition. With help, I have moved my exercise regime forward over the past few years from walking, to speed walking, to jogging on a treadmill at home. My doctor has recently given me the green light to jog outdoors over to a local school and do some moderate running of their track. To do this well, I needed a better pair of running shoes.

Here is why choosing a "neutral running shoe" could be a mistake for me. Since I have flat feet I need arch support, something "neutral running shoes" are not known for having much of. This new New Balance running shoe does have a modest built-in arch support; not a lot, but some. Most runners know what the word "pronation" means as it relates to running. Pronation describes how the foot rotates sideways through each step; the foot should rotate about 15 degrees toward the arch. Because I have flat feet, my feet overpronate toward the arch, putting my weight almost entirely on the big toe and the adjacent toe instead of being distributed evenly over all of my toes. Thus, walking, jogging or running for some length of time may result in two very tender and painful toes and toenails.

Like most running shoes these days, this pair has a "heel to toe" or a "midsole to toe" variance (I'm not sure what method New Balance uses to calculate this variance), which is how much higher the toe is from the heel or the midsole; this difference is also referred to as the "toe drop". Some running shoes have a 10mm to 12mm toe drop, so the modest 6mm differential in these New Balance running shoes actually makes it easier to land on the midsole or forefoot while running.

This running shoes not only has a modest arch, which not all "neutral running shoes" have, but it also has a relatively wide sole at the midsole of 4½", which does provide some stability for walkers/runners like me. Having these two pluses built into these New Balance running shoes, I decided to put them to the test. I've been walking on our treadmill and jogging/running on the school track for about a month and so far I am generally pleased with this pair of New Balance Vazee Pace running shoes. Only time with tell whether they will be suitable for the long haul.ctually makes it easier to land on the midsole or forefoot while running.

I got these to put prescription lenses in, and yes, I did look at the measurements, but I decided I could also return them if they didn't happen to fit my face properly.

The measurements from the left corner to the right corner (where the cat eye peaks) are about 6" wide. The lenses themselves are about 2 1/7" wide and 1 6/7" tall. The coloration is a lot bit darker in person. There's also a gold rim around the upper part of the glasses you can seem a lot more prominently than in the images.

PROS:
-Fairly sturdy for what you get.
-Really cute look.

CONS:
-Didn't fit my particular face shape.
-The tortoiseshell pattern is several shades darker in person. It's actually a noticeable difference.
-There is a gold rim you can hardly see in the images, but it's very prominent in person.
-Wouldn't recommend for casual non-prescriptive use since the glasses get a terrible glare on them.

I will keep wearing the shoes since they do support my feet and the right foot is perfect.  Someone suggested a heel insert which I have never needed in other shoes. I grew up with "Blundies" in Australia.
Bought a pair n the U.S. about 2-years ago.
Wore them a couple of times and then put them in storage.
Took them out this weekend to do some gardening and noticed chunks of black stuff on the ground.
Turns out it was the soles coming apart.
I've attached pics ... as you can see the leather is virtually brand new ... which it is ... but the soles are shot.

Spoke with a Customer Service rep from Blundstones U.S.A. and they've sent me a form to ship back the boots "to be reviewed".
I'm assuming they are well aware of the disintegrating soles issue as they address it in the form ... see below.

--------------------------
Letter from Blundstone U.S.A.

"Dear Blundstone Consumer,

Sorry to hear about the problem with your Blundstone boots. Please be aware that Blundstone boots carry a 2-year warranty against defects.

Blundstone boots are very durable; but will eventually wear out over time.

The boots cannot be re-soled due to the method of construction.

“Hydrolysis” is the breakdown of Poly Urethane, which can occur when boots are stored away for a long time. It is rare, but it does happen. When it does occur the outsole will start to deteriorate. If you feel your boots have succumbed to this, please send them back to the address below for quality inspection. If the boots are found defective we will replace them.

Please allow 2 weeks from receipt of boots to process your replacement.

Please fill out the following information to help us to assist you: ...

---------------------------

I really hope:

1. They REPLACE my boots;

2. They've IMPROVED their quality control.

I'll let you folks know of the outome.

========== UPDATE July 17, 2015 ===========

Today I received a new pair to replace my old/ defective ones from the U.S. distributors.

Kudos to them for recognizing there is a MAJOR DEFECT in these shoes and willing to replace them ... overall an awful business model.

Reading the WARNING (see attached) ... it states ..." ...If stored for extended periods, footwear should be stored in AIR CONDITIONED PREMISES. Failure to observe these precautions can lead to premature deterioration ..."

Ummm, while they're at it, they might as well have included ... "Only wear on premium, cashmere carpet ensuring the fibres are handpicked by virgins from nubile goats feasting on pristine pastures from the Kush mountain region above an altitude of 20,000 feet."

What a crock ... I though I bought a pair of Blundstones ... the type of shoes my mates and I grew up with back in the day ... which took a heap of punishment & lasted for years ... not something work gear needs to be kept in air conditioned comfort.

Based on that, and the fact that I also had to pay another $12 to ship back the shoes, not to mention the inconvenience & wasted time, I will definitely NOT RECOMMEND you purchase these shoes.

I just hope the new pair don't "deteriorate" as the last ones did ... in which case I don't hold any hope of them being replaced again.

These boots are in the middle pictured next to my camel leather boots and dark brown suede boots.
I went ahead and got my exact size (7.5) since a half-size up was out of stock, and it fits just fine. The problem? The color was NOTHING like the picture. I ordered the brown, which as you can see is the color of milk chocolate-- a nice rich, medium shade of brown. Maybe a hint of red. Just a shade or so darker than the boots on the left. What I GOT was more like dark chocolate-- as in, almost black. I briefly wondered if my mom had ordered the wrong color, but the color I received isn't shown in any of these pictures. It most closely resembles the "Brown PU" shade from this model: http://www.amazon.com/West-Blvd-Phoenix-Slouch-Slouchy/dp/B00NR7VQRO/ref=pd_sim_309_6?ie=UTF8&refRID=0288V3ZCR0TBYF8X3KJK. In fact, the box says that the shoe is "Brown PU" when we ordered simply "Brown". The exact same color on the other model is called Tan PU, but since the tan on this model actually looks tan, I'm not sure ordering the tan would solve my problem either. It looks like they simply only have this darker color of brown and posted the wrong picture for it... which is an issue, because I got these boots to match another item of mine.

Other notes: The transition between the heel and the ankle is incredibly awkward. It feels like there is a shoe inside the boot, and the "leg" portion of the boot is merely a loose leather sock coming up from it. Because of the structureless "sock" feeling, the leg portion easily slips down and wrinkles at the ankle. Yes, all boots have more structure in the feet-- but the difference in these boots is much more obvious. They probably need some thick socks/boot cuffs to hold them up.
Obviously, unless you haven't read other reviews, it's not actually thigh-high. The top of the "flap" portion just barely passes over the knee... still, they're taller than most boots and look great with the flap turned down. Unfortunately the flap covers the first "belt" decoration, but you can see the second one.
Finally, I was really hoping for a thin foot on the boot, since the "squashed beanbag" look from my hiking boots was what caused me to purchase these. I hate it when my feet look wide from the top. These are a huge improvement, but still a little squashed on the inner curve of my foot. Maybe I got have really thin feet... if you have wide feet, this will probably be perfect if not a little snug. But for me, I was hoping for a little more structure.th the flap turned down. I have been buying Skechers for a few years now, and I feel they have had shorter and shorter lifespans as time has gone on. I have high arches and somewhat wide feet and for many years Saucony neutral shoes were my go-to running shoes. When the first versions of Saucony Ride came out I found the soles far too soft so that my landings felt unstable.  But when at last the Ride 6 was made available, I knew I'd found my way back to Saucony.  Though I have always worn a size 6.5 street shoe and a 7 med. running shoe, I had to buy a 7.5 medium in the Ride 6 in the citron color.  Because they were so comfortable ( they do not have a lot of arch support, so I replaced the factory insoles with arch insoles), I ordered another pair in silver-gray/green in a 7.5 medium but, upon running in them, I found they were half size too long and altered my stride. Since it was too late to send them back, I've kept them for dog walking but it seems wrong and is rather frustrating to discover that an athletic shoe company like Saucony would manufacture shoes that vary in size depending on which color one buys.  To my mind, this is the source of customers' various reviews with regard to fit; there is a lack of consistency when it comes to sizing.

Overall I'm happy with these boots. For $20, I think they're definitely worth buying. Hopefully this review will help you decide whether they're worth it or not for you.

Fit

After reading the reviews that said the boots ran small, I ordered an 8.5 instead of my usual 8. I think I could have gone with an 8, as the 8.5 is pretty roomy. On the upside, the half size bigger will allow me to wear thick socks comfortably, so it works. My calves are about 14" around, and I have enough room in the boots to tuck jeans in. However, they are snug with jeans, and the boots themselves don't stretch, so if your calves are any wider than 16" these boots will probably not be comfortable.

Durability

Since it's still August, I haven't been able to wear the boots out and about yet. I've spent a couple days walking around in them, folding them, scrunching them, etc. and they aren't showing any wear. Definitely not a snow boot, but for walking they seem to hold up fine.

Style

There's some issues in this category that cause the boots to lose a star, in my opinion. When you wear them as-is (over the knee), they look kind of... clunky. If the boots were more fitted around the knee they'd look better. However, when you fold the top part down, they look a lot more flattering. The cuff hits right below the knee and gives the boot a much better shape. There's still something off about the way the boots look from the front, like the ankle is too thick, possibly due to the zipper on the side. Even so, I love the fantasy look of these boots. From the side they look great.

Final thoughts

I would definitely buy these boots again. At $20, there's not much to lose. And they look really cool.

I've used Chaco products for 10 years, three continents, and in almost a dozen countries. I've used Chaco sandals during that time as a Peace Corps volunteer in Africa, on my feet in some incredibly remote and rugged terrain. I've used Chacos sandals as a surf photographer in Costa Rica where they were constantly soaked with salt water and buried in sand. I'm wearing a pair, right now as I type this, that I've had since 2006, and am about to re-glue to soles to the tread. I think it's safe to say that I know Chaco footwear, and I've liked them more than any other sandal and shoe brand, ever. When it comes to the Outcross Lace Water Shoe, Chaco has disappointed me. Don't get me wrong, they're solidly constructed, the Vibram outsole is sticky, and so far the upper and the lower part of the shoe has stood up to everything a National Park Ranger working in South West Utah can throw at them (wearing a bullet-proof vest, full duty gear, etc.). Yet, the lacing system has me confused. There are so many other brands of shoes and sandals out there using a lacing system that works, and Chaco tried to re-invent the wheel for some reason the way they've designed theirs. I had my Outcross Lace Water Shoes for two weeks, wore them maybe 10 times, and the plastic cinch for the quick laces broke. The way they're designed, when you pull up on the laces to cinch them tight, it stresses the plastic cinch and bends and breaks it, releasing it from the strangely large amount of fabric that keeps it attached to the tongue of the shoe. This means that the tongue of the shoes falls below the lace, and the lace is now up against your foot, chafing terribly if not noticed and corrected consistently. Ultimately, I like the shoes, but the lacing system is terrible, and I'll probably just end up ripping the laces out and installing some after-market laces or something, because these are awful. Seriously, though, other than the laces, everyone who wears Keen's around me asks where I got my shoes,and compliments that they don't look weird like Keen's, and have better grip and utility climbing/hiking/working on a boat than Keen's.

I purchased these shoes to do my first re-enactment event. Not having the money or time to get the real deal these seemed a good alternative. I read the reviews and noted the sizing issues that two others had and since I too wear a size 10-10 1/2 I took their advice and ordered a size up(12/13). Even though I was wearing heavy wool stockings and 2 pairs of shorty socks and stuffed the toes with paper they were still big. My advice is to order the size that matches your feet and do your best to stretch them if needed. I ended up only wearing them for a few hours due to the feeling of walking in clown shoes, just way too big. I had about two inches of space between my big toe and the shoe tip, and was just big all the way around.

That being said, I was pleasantly surprised by the quality given that they are poly and not real leather. They seem well built, have a close to authentic appearance (the buckles were dark gray not brass or silver colored and the \\"leather\\" was a very dark gray) and, other than the size issue, comfortable. The soles are pretty slick though. For the price these are an excellent value if you only need to wear them a few times a year. I would get another pair if the need arises. They would've got a 4 star if not for the fit and return policy. If they didn't have a restocking fee I would have returned them and being in a pinch didn't help either.

I've been wearing Asics for running for about 15 years and have always been extremely satisfied. Lately though, I've been terribly disappointed mainly because of the sizing issues.

I then tried the 21s and they were so narrow and short even in a wide width and I have always been a standard width. Tried the nimbus next and they were great in the toe box, still very short in length but caused numbness in the balls of my feet. The 1000 3 were short and really stiff. The cumulus were really short like my foot measures a 6 1/2 and an 8 was to short. The gel exalt slipped in the heel and were very narrow.

So here I am with the 2000 3. I always wear a 7 standard width in street shoes and up until this shake up was a 7 1/2 standard width in all Asics shoes. I decided to go to a running store for help out of sheer frustration. On a foot measurer I am a 6 1/2 standard width but was fitted in an 8 Wide in these. I really hope Asics gets it together soon because color selection and in stock options suck in wide.

I had some reservations in the beginning. Could this product really work? Isn't it kinda pricey? I mean, really...$22 so I don’t have to tie my shoelaces. Really??? Then they were delivered.

First thing I did was look for the instructions. Ha! There were none. No big problem. I just Googled “Zubits Instructions” and there they were. But wouldn’t you think for twenty-two bucks there would be instructions? I did. Seems you would want your customers to be able to start using your product right out of the box. That’s just good business sense.

If you think all you have to do is re-lace your shoes to accommodate the Zubits, you would be wrong. It is a trial and error fit and the instructions (now that I had them) even suggests you may have to tie, retie, and retie your laces again for the best fit.

Finally, my shoes were laced into the Zubits and it worked as advertized...sorta. You have to be careful when closing the Zubits that they do not grab anything between the underneath side of the Zubits and the top surface of your shoe. The magnets are strong and if you are not careful, they will grab the surface of your shoe and not provide the needed magnetic seal.

Knowing what I now know, I would not recommend Zubits...unless it is really-really worth $22 to you not have to have to deal with shoelaces ever-ever again. Personally, I think you are trading one hassle for another.

====================== The Next Day ======================

I tried them in earnest...REALLY. I figured if the Zubits would keep my laces from getting snagged when riding my bike, it might be worth the $22, but I never got that far. I took five steps out of the house and the Zubits separated. I reconnected the Zubits, took four steps and they separated again. I am returning them today. Too bad.

I ordered the Rosie, Jenna, Jeanine, Fenna, Sarina, the Laser. ........ I have some foot issues...I get a hard knot in the center of the ball of my feet if shoes don't fit correctly, so fit and comfort was crucial.

Although the same size was ordered, some of these shoes fit tighter than others. The toe box varied on each style as well. I've written reviews on each one indicating the difference in fit.

What feels good for one person may not feel great for another so it's difficult to gain much from shoe reviews unless you understand your feet...toe box requirements, arch support, heel height. I have used this bag for over a month. And here are my thoughts:

COLOR - I actually bought the black, sand, ambrosia and periwinkle colored purses because I wasn't sure which bags I would want to keep. The colors are all true as pictured. But I ended up keeping the black and sand colors just because they are the most versatile. That said - the colors are all nice - so choose the one you will wear most.

SIZE: I can fit my iPhone 6, my smallish wallet, and some other small items (lipstick, pens, small bottle of advil etc.) but I am unable to fit my sunglass case or anything bigger. So I can't rely on this as my everyday purse when I will need to carry more items... Instead I use this bag when I am out for the afternoon or evening and don't need to carry a lot. But I use my big purse for everything else. Also something to note, when I am able to stuff more in the purse, it gets too weighted and the thin strap hurts my shoulder. So this purse really is meant to just carry the bare essentials.

HANGS: This purse is meant to hang cross body. When you hang it on your shoulder and let it hang straight down, it doesn't really hang right, it kind of hangs on an angle. So this bag can be hung straight down, but it will feel more comfortable hung cross body.

LENGTH: I am 6' tall. I have it on the longest length and it does fit correctly. There is around 6" of play, So this purse will work for most women,

LINING / POCKETS: The pockets are nice (I like keeping lipstick, pens in the front pocket; feminine products in the interior pocket; and receipts in the outside back flap). And the lining is cute.

SCENT: of the 4 bags I purchased, 2 of them had a strong smell (maybe from the glue?) when I opened them up. But after a couple of days the scent went away.

SUM: At this price-point ($30-$50 a bag), you can buy 4 bags for the price of one of the "nicer" bags. That is why I felt totally comfortable keeping 2 of them to wear with different outfits. I wish the bag "magically" held more, but in reality that would just make it a bigger bag. It is both cute and classy, and I am glad I bought it. I just wish they had designed the bag so it would hang straight when I don't wear it cross body. I hope this is helpful to you!keeping 2 of them to wear with different outfits. I'm pretty disappointed with this shoe. I bought it because I'm experiencing metatarsal pain in one foot and this shoe is reportedly one of those that will help alleviate that. I read a lot of reviews on this shoe, including those contained in other sites related to shoes that are good orthotic type shoes. I was also looking for a shoe made in the USA. New Balance is the parent company and many of their shoes are made in the USA. This one isn't. Given the data accompanying the description on Amazon, I thought it was. This shoe is made in China.

If you've worn the fine running shoes made in the USA by New Balance as I have, one may have a tendency to compare those shoes to this one. Don't. They're not at all alike. This shoe is light weight, but in my opinion that's where the "good" stops. It looks to me to be a hard formed plastic sole attached to a not so comfortable leather upper. It fit longer than expected even after I carefully measured my feet and compared the "how does this shoe fit?" on several web sites. The insole is very thin and provides next to nothing in the way of cushioning and arch support.

Bottom line; this shoe gets very good reviews from a lot of people, but it's not doing the job for me. If I hadn't worn it to work for a full day after trying it on, I would send it back.

I have been wearing Keens for years, but always the fabric strap/rubber sole kind. When I saw that Keens now come in this leather design, I was psyched. I actually had on my previous Keens while I was making the online order, so I checked the size and ordered that size (9). For context: I wear a 9 in almost all footwear, besides a few athletic shoes (Puma and Nike), in which I wear a 9.5. When these Keens arrived, I loved their look, but my heel hung off the back considerably, and I couldn't make them work at all. I also felt like even with wiggling my toes and tightening the straps of the shoe, I couldn't get my toes to a place where they stayed toward the front of the shoe as I walked (and therefore contributing to my heel hanging so far off the back). I was confused, but figured this style just ran small, and exchanged them for the 9.5. When the 9.5 arrived, my heel hung off the back of the shoe maybe slightly less, but still too much that it affected the comfort and aesthetic of my foot in the shoe (with every step I took, I could not only see but also feel that something was off and my heel was too far back). I put in an exchange for the 10 (even though I have never worn a size 10 in any shoe, ever), but I think the problem might be the shoe. Unlike the previous Keens that I have owned (the Whisper Sandal in fabric), the heel bed of this shoe is totally flat, rather than with a slight curve upwards at the back of the heel. That slight curve in the Keens I currently wear seems to function to keep my toes toward the front of the shoe and, overall, keep my foot in the right place. I think the problem with these Keens is that the heel bed is completely flat, with no curve at the back, so there is nothing to keep my toes toward the front of the shoe. I think the problem with the 10s will be that there is way too much space between my toes and the front of the shoe, but I'm still willing to give them a try -- I really like the way Keens look in leather!

I've owned dozens of Ray Bans, and more than my fair share of Wayfarers. That said, I'm pretty familiar with BL's quality, and what a pair of authentic Wayfarers should feel like - and unfortunately in this case, these were fakes.

Real Wayfarers frames are made of acetate, have a nice smooth finish, and a nice weight to them. The ones I received were cheap plastic, and had ridges running down the top of both arms. More importantly, RB uses glass lenses. The ones I got were extremely thin and light plastic. Essentially, I received a nice-looking pair of gas station shades.

I will say, though, that from a distance they looked good. And the packaging looked spot on. Had I not been familiar with RB's products, I might've been fooled enough to keep them.

So be careful - I still love Amazon, but be warned that there are fakes out there. If the price is too good to be true (in this case, about $60, as opposed to about $100), then it just might be...
